h:
You have faith.

Christ is coming back.

Not to bear the cross again, but to establish His Kingdom.

What exactly are you expecting to happen when He does?

For many Christians, the ending is already settled. Christ returns. The faithful leave. Heaven is the destination. Earth is the place God wraps up before moving on.

The answer comes quickly. Fast answers usually reveal inherited ones.

Before asking whether a doctrine is comforting, ask whether it is true.

Open the text. Forget what you’ve heard. Start at the beginning.

Nobody Reads Without Assumptions

The question is whether those assumptions came from Moses and the prophets, or from a nineteenth-century theological system most readers have never heard of.

John Nelson Darby, an Anglo-Irish Plymouth Brethren minister, built what he called dispensationalism in the 1830s, a system dividing history into distinct eras, treating Israel and the church as separate tracks, with a pretribulation rapture as the hinge. Believers exit before the tribulation. The earth receives judgment. The church doesn’t go through the fire because it leaves first.

No church father articulated the modern pretribulation rapture that Darby systematized. The early Christian martyrs, already living through tribulation, were not waiting for extraction from it. The gap between Darby and the nearest patristic predecessor runs roughly 1,500 years. This is not a recovery of something ancient. It is an innovation.

The innovation needed a way to spread. C.I. Scofield provided it. His Scofield Reference Bible, published in 1909, embedded Darby’s entire system into the footnotes of the King James text, sitting directly beneath scripture, on the same page, in the same binding. A reader could not always tell where God’s word ended and Darby’s commentary began.

Dallas Theological Seminary gave the system academic respectability. Hal Lindsey’s “The Late Great Planet Earth” (1970) turned it into mass-market prophecy. The Left Behind series sold 80 million copies and turned the theology into story, then into background radiation.

By the time most believers open the Bible for the first time, the story has already been told to them. They are not asking what the story is. They are looking for where the story confirms the one they already know.

The text is no longer leading the reader. The reader is leading the text.

God Never Called Creation the Problem

Go back further than Darby. Go back to Genesis 1.

God creates in sequence, light, land, sea, vegetation, sky, creatures, and finally humanity. After each stage: good. After humanity is placed in the garden in the image of God, after creation is complete: very good.

God creates earth. He creates bodies. He places His image-bearers in a material world and walks among them.

Adam is not given a body.

Adam becomes a living being through one (Genesis 2:7).

Scripture never presents the body as a temporary container for the real person.

The embodied human being is the person.

So what went wrong?

Not matter. Not bodies. Not creation. Not the physical world.

Sin.

What enters after the fall is not the burden of being embodied in a material world. What enters is death, exile, corruption, alienation, and the curse. These are the specific problems introduced in Genesis 3. And if you read what follows, the Torah, the prophets, the psalms, the New Testament, you are reading the story of God methodically reversing every one of them.

Not abandoning the creation where they occurred.

Reversing them.

Death enters. God promises resurrection. Exile enters. God promises return. Corruption enters. God promises renewal. Alienation enters. God promises presence. The curse enters. God promises restoration.

Even the rebellious powers that corrupted the nations do not stand outside that story. They too are judged, displaced, and replaced.

The story never changes. From Genesis to Revelation, God is undoing everything sin introduced.

The Bible is not the story of God rescuing souls from Earth.

It is the story of God restoring His creation and dwelling with humanity forever.

God Has Been Moving Toward Humanity

Notice the direction of redemption.

Humanity never rebuilds Babel successfully.

Humanity never climbs back into Eden.

Humanity never ascends into heaven by its own effort.

At every stage, God is the One who descends.

He descends upon Sinai.

He fills the tabernacle.

He fills the temple.

He becomes flesh.

His Spirit descends at Pentecost.

The New Jerusalem descends from heaven.

The direction never changes.

Grace always moves downward before humanity can ever move upward.

The thread through the whole Bible answers one question: where does God dwell?

In the garden, before the fall, God walks among humanity. The Hebrew of Genesis 3:8 — מתהלך (mithallek) — implies habitual movement. This was not a one-time appearance. God walked with humanity in the created order, in the ordinary pattern of days.

Sin breaks the proximity. Humanity is exiled. But notice what God does next.

Sin creates distance. God answers by crossing it.

Exodus 25:8, God gives Moses the instructions for the tabernacle: “Let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.” The Hebrew is שכן (shakan) — to settle, to tabernacle. God is not withdrawing to a permanent heavenly address. He is establishing a presence in the middle of the wilderness camp, in a portable structure that travels with the people through the desert.

The tabernacle settles among the people. The temple roots that presence in the heart of the nation. When Solomon dedicates it, the glory of God fills the house so completely that the priests cannot stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10-11). God’s presence settles into a house in the middle of a city in the middle of a nation.

Then the nation breaks covenant. Ezekiel 10 records the consequence, the glory lifting off the temple, departing in stages, moving east. One of the most devastating passages in the prophetic literature. But Ezekiel doesn’t end there. Chapter 43 records the vision of the glory returning. The same movement, reversed. The glory returns. The distance begins to close.

Then comes the moment the whole pattern was pointing toward.

John 1:14 - “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” The Greek is ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen). He tabernacled among us. John is not speaking loosely. He is placing Jesus in the line of the tabernacle and the temple, the same divine presence that descended on Sinai, that filled Solomon’s house, that Ezekiel watched depart and return, now in human flesh, walking the roads of Galilee.

After the resurrection, the presence extends. At Pentecost the Spirit comes. 1 Corinthians 3:16 - “You are God’s temple and God’s Spirit dwells in you.” The community of believers becomes the place where God’s presence dwells. The presence that moved from garden to tabernacle to temple to incarnate Son now takes up residence in a people.

And then Revelation 21:3 - “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and He will dwell with them.” The Greek is σκηνή (skēnē). Tabernacle. The same root John used in chapter 1. The same movement. God tabernacling with humanity, permanently, on a renewed earth, with no more exile, no more curtain, no more departure.

The direction of the Bible is consistent across every testament, every covenant, every stage of the story.

Humanity is not ascending toward God.

God is moving toward humanity.

Revelation 21 is the arrival point the entire story was always aimed at.

Heaven Was Never the Ending

With that thread in place, the closing chapters of Scripture read as climax, not consolation.

Revelation 5:10 - the redeemed “will reign on the earth.”

Revelation 21:2 - “I saw the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God.” Down. The city descends to the earth. Not believers ascending to heaven, the new creation arriving on the earth. The direction is not upward and away. It is downward and toward.

The promise is not confined to a single verse in a single book. It runs across the biblical tradition.

In Psalm 37, David returns to it again and again. “Those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land” (v. 9). “The meek shall inherit the earth” (v. 11). “Those blessed by Him shall inherit the land” (v. 22). “The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever” (v. 29). The wicked appear to prosper now, but the earth belongs to the righteous at the end.

1 Enoch 5:7 echoes the same hope: “For the elect there shall be light and joy and peace, and they shall inherit the earth.”

Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount with Matthew 5:5: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” He does not replace the promise. He reaffirms it.

David. Enoch. Jesus.

The earth.

Romans 8:19-21 - creation itself waits in eager expectation and “will be liberated from its bondage to decay.” Paul does not offer creation an escape from corruption. He offers it liberation from corruption. Creation is not the problem. It is the patient waiting for the promise.

Acts 3:21 - God will “restore everything.” The Greek is ἀποκατάστασις (apokatastasis). Restoration of all things. Not relocation. Not replacement. Restoration.

Isaiah 65:17-25 - the new creation described in the most material terms in scripture. Vineyards planted and eaten from. Houses built and inhabited. The wolf and the lamb together. No mystical abstraction. Embodied, agricultural, creaturely life on an earth that has been made new.

This is the same note played across five centuries of prophetic literature. God is restoring the creation He called very good. Not escaping it. Not burning the draft and beginning somewhere else. Restoring it.

Jesus repeatedly speaks of His followers receiving a kingdom, sitting on thrones, and reigning with Him (Luke 22:28–30; Revelation 3:21). Those promises make little sense if the final hope is simply existing forever in heaven as disembodied souls. Kings rule somewhere. Thrones belong to kingdoms. Christ’s promise is not merely that His people will be with Him. It is that they will reign with Him.

The reader who arrives at Revelation 21 having followed the thread from Genesis should not be surprised.

They should recognize where they are.

If Heaven Were the Goal, God Didn’t Need the Resurrection

If heaven is the final destination, if the goal is for souls to exist in a spiritual realm with God forever, then the resurrection is unnecessary.

Death already accomplishes the transfer. The soul departs the body, goes to God, and the story ends there.

So why does God raise bodies?

Why does Paul call death the “last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26)? If death carries you to the true destination, it is not an enemy to be defeated. It is a doorway to be embraced.

Why does Paul spend the longest single argument in all of his letters, the entirety of 1 Corinthians 15, defending bodily resurrection against people who preferred a purely spiritual interpretation?

Why does Revelation describe the new creation as a physical place with a river, a tree, gates, and nations?

Why does Isaiah give the new creation vineyards?

Why does Acts 3 use a Greek word that means restoration?

None of this makes sense if leaving creation was always the plan.

Paul gives the answer in one phrase: “Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits. The first sheaf of a harvest is the guarantee of the rest. Whatever happened to Jesus becomes the destiny of those who belong to Him. His resurrection is the future of every believer, revealed ahead of time.

Resurrection is not God’s backup plan. It is God’s declaration that death never had the final word.

He Kept the Body

The resurrection doesn’t just prove Jesus conquered death. It reveals what God intends to save.

He kept the wounds. Thomas is invited to touch them (John 20:27). He kept the hands, the feet, the voice, Mary recognizes Him when he speaks her name (John 20:16). He kept the appetite. He eats fish on the beach in front of the disciples (Luke 24:42-43). When they mistake him for a ghost, he corrects them: “A ghost does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have” (Luke 24:39).

He is transformed. He appears through locked doors (John 20:19). His body is imperishable in ways it was not before. But He is not a spirit. He is not a disembodied soul. He is the same person, recognizable, touchable, physically present, in a body that death could not hold.

He ascended in that body. The angels at the ascension gave the disciples watching from below one piece of information: “This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go” (Acts 1:11).

Jesus is not the exception to what resurrection looks like. He is the firstfruits, the first sheaf that determines the shape of the harvest. The promise to believers is the same trajectory. Not escape from the body. Transformation of it. Not departure from the earth. Return to it.

The body was not the problem.

The body is part of the promise.

What Happens After Death Is Not the End of the Story

Before the resurrection comes another question.

What happens when a believer dies, before the resurrection?

Scripture is clear. Believers are with Christ after death. Paul writes in Philippians 1:23 that departing and being with Christ is “better by far.” Jesus tells the thief on the cross: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). 2 Corinthians 5:8, to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord.

Believers who die are with Christ. Scripture is clear about that. But Scripture is equally clear that the story does not end there.

The saints under the altar in Revelation 6:10 are present with God and still crying out, “How long?” They are waiting for something. What they are waiting for is what Revelation 21 describes: the resurrection, the new creation, the permanent address. The intermediate state is not the destination. It is the interval before the promise is fulfilled.

For many modern Christians, the intermediate state has quietly replaced the resurrection as the center of Christian hope, treating “with Christ after death” as the full promise, when the text treats it as the penultimate chapter before the real ending.

The disembodied state is the condition of the dead before the resurrection.

The resurrection body on a renewed earth is the promise.

Christ Himself leaves no ambiguity: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

The theology you believe determines the world you build.

If you believe you’re leaving, you’ll live like a tenant.

If you believe God is restoring creation, you’ll live like an heir.

The new creation will be populated by the same people who lived in this one, transformed, glorified, imperishable, but continuous with who they became. The work done here does not evaporate at death. It goes into the person. And the person comes back.

Which means art matters, beauty is no longer decoration. It becomes an act of faith in the world God intends to restore.

Justice is no longer temporary damage control. It becomes a witness to the Kingdom that is coming.

Families matter. Craftsmanship matters. Stewardship of creation matters. Faithfulness in unseen work matters. The body matters. Learning to love well matters. None of it is preparation for an exit. It is preparation for an inheritance.

The conclusion of Paul’s resurrection theology is not withdrawal. It’s work:

“Therefore, my dear brothers and sisters, stand firm. Let nothing move you. Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

The resurrection makes faithfulness an investment. Escape makes it an evacuation.

The Bible begins with God walking among humanity in a garden.

It ends with God dwelling among humanity in a city where the river of life still flows and the tree still bears its fruit.

So build accordingly.

Therefore pray thus:

“Our Father in the heavens,

let Your name be hallowed.

Let Your kingdom come,

let Your will be done,

as in heaven, also upon earth.

Give us this day our daily bread,

and forgive us our debts,

as we also have forgiven our debtors.

And lead us not into temptation,

but deliver us from the evil one.” - Matthew 6:9-13:
